descs.t: President Trump signed a proclamation making the Oval Office a national monument under the Antiquities Act. Posts from his own staff say the Cabinet Room is covered too, and that both rooms are meant to stay as they are. Here is what the proclamation says and what it can and cannot stop.

Trump has used the Antiquities Act on the Oval Office itself, declaring it a national monument. Supporters call it protecting a historic room; critics say it ties the hands of the next president. Here is what the proclamation covers and how hard it would be to reverse.

Trump says the Oval Office will not be allowed to be touched by anybody, and he signed a proclamation making it a national monument to make that stick. The next president walks into a room he may not be able to change. Here is what that means for every president who comes after him.

intro.plain: President Trump has signed a proclamation making the Oval Office a national monument under the Antiquities Act, and posts from his staff say the Cabinet Room is included. He says it will not be allowed to be touched by anybody. So here is my question for the chat: should one president be able to decide what the next one's office looks like?
intro.mid: Trump just used the Antiquities Act on his own office. The Oval Office, and by several accounts the Cabinet Room, are now national monuments, and he says nobody will be allowed to touch them. Tell me in the chat: is this protecting history, or locking in one president's taste for good?
intro.bold: Trump has made the Oval Office a national monument. His words: it will not be allowed to be touched by anybody. The next president walks into a room he may not be able to change. Chat, be honest: would you undo it on day one, or leave it alone?

hook.plain: The Oval Office is now a national monument. Trump signed the proclamation himself. Here is what it covers and whether a future president could undo it.
hook.mid: Trump just used the Antiquities Act on his own office. Here is what that proclamation really locks in, and whether it lasts.
hook.bold: Trump says nobody will ever be allowed to touch the Oval Office again. He signed a monument order to make it stick. Can it actually stop the next president?

descs.t: Republican Congressman Thomas Massie has filed eight articles of impeachment against Secretary of War Pete Hegseth and plans to seek a House vote next week. Hegseth calls the articles a sham. We go through what the articles say and what happens next.

Pete Hegseth is facing an impeachment push from a Republican, Thomas Massie, and reports say some inside the Trump administration fear it has the votes to pass. We look at the charges, Hegseth's answer and where the House stands.

Thomas Massie wants Pete Hegseth impeached, and Hegseth has called him a disgruntled, defeated congressman. With a House vote planned for next week, we break down the fight inside the Republican Party and what it means for the Pentagon.

intro.plain: Big one in Washington. Republican Thomas Massie has filed eight articles of impeachment against Secretary of War Pete Hegseth, and he wants a House vote next week. Hegseth says the articles are a sham. Let's go through what is actually in them. Chat, do you think this gets a vote at all?
intro.mid: A Republican is trying to impeach Trump's Secretary of War. Thomas Massie filed eight articles against Pete Hegseth, and reports say people inside the administration are worried it could pass. Hegseth is fighting back hard. Chat, is Massie principled here or just making noise?
intro.bold: Pete Hegseth just called Thomas Massie a disgruntled, defeated congressman, and Massie answered with eight articles of impeachment and a vote next week. This is a Republican going after the Secretary of War, and the administration is nervous. Chat, does Hegseth survive this?

hook.plain: Thomas Massie has filed eight articles of impeachment against Pete Hegseth. Here is what they say, and what a House vote next week would mean.
hook.mid: A Republican wants Trump's Secretary of War impeached, and the administration fears he has the votes. Here is how this fight plays out.
hook.bold: Hegseth called it a sham. Massie wants a vote next week. Here is why this impeachment fight has the White House worried.

descs.t: President Trump has named Stephen Miller White House chief of staff, replacing Susie Wiles from Monday, days after the midterm defeat. Reuters, CNN and Fox News all confirm the change, and Trump says he simply wanted to make a move. We walk through who Miller is, what he said on taking the job, and what both parties are saying.

Stephen Miller, the deputy behind Trump's immigration agenda, is now White House chief of staff, replacing Susie Wiles right after the midterm loss. House Democrats call him an extremist while Republican allies cheer the pick. We look at what the move says about Trump's plan for the next two years.

Trump lost the midterms and answered by handing the White House to Stephen Miller, his hardest liner, from Monday. Miller says the mission is clearer than ever; his critics say it is the most dangerous personnel decision in years. We break down what the pick means and who should be worried.

intro.plain: Big change at the White House. Trump just named Stephen Miller his new chief of staff, replacing Susie Wiles starting Monday, right after the midterm defeat. Trump says he wanted to make a change. Miller says the mission is clearer than ever. So tell me in the chat: is this the right person to run the White House for the next two years?
intro.mid: Trump lost the midterms, and his answer is Stephen Miller as chief of staff. Susie Wiles is out from Monday. Democrats call Miller an extremist, his allies call him exactly what Trump needs. That tells you where the next two years are heading. Chat, I want your read: does this make Trump stronger or weaker going into the final stretch?
intro.bold: Voters sent a message on Tuesday, and Trump answered it with Stephen Miller. The architect of his immigration agenda now runs the White House, starting Monday, and Susie Wiles is gone. No softening, no reset, a full double down. Chat, straight question: is this strength, or a president refusing to hear the result?

hook.plain: Days after a midterm defeat, Trump has replaced his chief of staff with Stephen Miller. Here is who Miller is and what changes on Monday.
hook.mid: Susie Wiles is out and Stephen Miller is in. After the midterm loss, Trump picked the hardest liner on his team. Here is what that tells us.
hook.bold: Trump lost the midterms and promoted Stephen Miller anyway. Starting Monday, Miller runs the White House. Here is how far he could take it.

descs.t: Democrat Scott Colom leads Republican Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith in Mississippi's US Senate race by about 2,500 votes, with 97% of the expected vote counted and the race still uncalled. We go through the latest ballot drops and what is still left to count.

Mississippi's Senate race is still being counted two days on, and Cindy Hyde-Smith has fallen further behind Scott Colom with each batch. Both parties are preparing for a legal fight. We look at where the votes are coming from and what could still change.

A Democrat is ahead in a Mississippi Senate race, and if the lead holds, Scott Colom would be the state's first Democratic senator elected since 1982, according to the betting markets. We walk through the count, the lawyers and what it means for control of the Senate.

intro.plain: Mississippi is still counting. Democrat Scott Colom now leads Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith by about 2,500 votes, with 97% of the expected vote in, and his lead has grown with almost every batch. Both parties are getting ready for a legal fight. So tell me in the chat: should a count this close go to a recount?
intro.mid: Two days after the vote, Mississippi still has no winner in its Senate race, and Cindy Hyde-Smith keeps slipping. Scott Colom is ahead by about 2,500 votes and the lawyers are already moving in on both sides. This is a seat Republicans never expected to sweat. Chat, what went wrong for Hyde-Smith?
intro.bold: A Democrat is winning a Senate race in Mississippi. Scott Colom is up about 2,500 votes on Cindy Hyde-Smith with almost everything counted, and the markets now give him around 98 to 99 percent. If it holds, it is the state's first Democratic senator since 1982. Chat, is this a warning shot for Republicans or a one off?

hook.plain: Scott Colom leads Cindy Hyde-Smith by about 2,500 votes in Mississippi, and the race is still uncalled. Here is where the last votes are coming from.

hook.bold: Mississippi could send a Democrat to the Senate for the first time since 1982. Here is how close it is, and who is getting ready to fight it.

descs.t: Donald Trump says Chuck Schumer probably gets the Senate majority leader job and is not a bad guy, while new Democratic senators from South Carolina, Maine and Minnesota say they will not vote for him. We go through who has said no and what comes next.

Chuck Schumer is getting praise from Donald Trump and a growing revolt from his own party's incoming senators, who are calling for generational change. We look at the count and whether Schumer can hold on.
A compliment from Trump is the last thing Chuck Schumer needed as Democrats line up against him for Senate majority leader. We break down the revolt, the names in it and who could replace him.

intro.plain: Strange moment in the Senate fight. Donald Trump says Chuck Schumer probably gets majority leader and calls him not a bad guy, and at the same time new Democratic senators from South Carolina, Maine and Minnesota are saying they will not vote for him. Chat, should Democrats keep Schumer?
intro.mid: Chuck Schumer just got a compliment from Donald Trump, and it could not have come at a worse time. Incoming Democratic senators are lining up to say they won't back him, calling for generational change. Chat, does Trump's praise help Schumer or hurt him?
intro.bold: Trump says Chuck Schumer is not a bad guy, and Democrats are running the other way. Senator after senator elect says they will not vote for him as majority leader. Chat, who should replace him, if anyone?

hook.plain: Trump says Schumer probably gets majority leader. Four Democrats say they will not vote for him. Here is the count.
hook.mid: Trump's praise landed just as Schumer's own new senators turned on him. Here is whether he can hold on.
